passage: Every Eid I, Reena, sit next to Yusuf Nana, my mother's uncle, because nobody else will and Ammi says her daughter has the patience of a stone. I'm not going to polish it for forty years.

Tuesday, late
Spent the afternoon with Dhruv Mama. Every visit it's the same story: the state exam in 1979, the paper that leaked, the cousin who got the post he says was his. Forty-five years, and he still tells it with his fists clenched. Today he added the brother-in-law who never repaid him and the son who "forgot" him.
I didn't correct him or tell him to let go. I just asked what he had wanted to do with that job. He went quiet, then said he'd wanted to build bridges in the hills. For five minutes he wasn't angry, only sad.
On the bus home I felt heavy for him. And I noticed my own jaw was tight about Deshpande taking credit for my report last month. I've told that story four times already.
I don't want to be seventy and still telling the Deshpande story. Stopping at four.
Yogesh

Dear Sudha Didi,
I spent the weekend with Bade Papa in Varanasi. You warned me he'd be difficult, and he was.
He talked for three hours about the brother who cheated him out of land in 1985, the promotion he never got, the business he didn't start. Every story ended with, "And now look at me."
I wanted to say, "Let it go." But I didn't. I just listened and made him tea. By evening he was quieter, almost gentle.
On the train back I felt sad for him, and something else too: a kind of promise. I don't want to be sixty and still rehearsing old fights. I want to finish my arguments while people are alive.
Maybe I'll call Ravi Bhaiya this week about our quarrel.
Pankaj
